title: Belief And Identity, Answered Against The Sources
slot: Religious Education & Ethics (AQA GCSE Religious Studies)
objective: Answer the belief and identity question under assessment conditions, reporting two approved sources and comparing them, then mark your own answer against the checklist and name the line that would gain the next mark.

blocks.text: LAUNCH · Humanities · Week 7. Religious Education and Ethics. Belief And Identity, Answered Against The Sources.
Objective: answer the belief and identity question, reporting two approved sources and comparing them, then mark your own answer against the checklist.
Success evidence: one answer naming two sources, a checklist marked in your own hand with line numbers, and one next-mark line.
Every quotation comes from the approved source sheet. You report what a source teaches. You are not asked what you believe, and never about your family.
40 minutes. Offline.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Source sheets, question and checklist out before pupils sit. Nothing is handed round once writing has started.
stages.data-ta2: If a pupil offers what they or their family believe, name the source sheet in front of them and move on. Do not follow it up.

blocks.text: The same frame, now against the clock
You have used the report frame for three weeks.
Today it is timed, and today you mark your own answer.
The job has not changed. Name a source, report what it teaches, then compare.
The question is about belief and identity: how what a tradition teaches shapes who a person says they are.
You report that from the sheet. You never report it from yourself.
Read the question aloud once, then stop talking. The silence is part of the assessment condition.
You need the source sheet, the question, the checklist and a pencil.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Show both answers, then take them down before writing starts.

blocks.text: Two answers, one mark apart
Answer A says belief makes people who they are.
It could have been written without reading the sheet, so it earns nothing.
Answer B says source one describes dress as a daily sign of belonging.
It names a source, so an examiner can check it.

items: 3 · set it beside the second source.
4 · label the point shared or different.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Model the opening two sentences only, then stop. Do not model a whole answer.

blocks.text: The opening two sentences
I read the question twice before I write anything.
Then I write: source one teaches that daily prayer marks a person as part of a community.
That names the source and uses a reporting verb.
Then source two: source two teaches that identity is carried in what a person chooses not to do.

blocks.caption: The same four steps, written under the clock
blocks.title: The frame, timed
blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows: name the source, report what it teaches, compare it with the second, label the point

blocks.text: Two sentences, two sources, and no opinion yet.
Stop after the second report and say why. Under time pressure pupils reach for judgement in the third sentence.
Notice the verbs. Teaches and describes, never think or feel.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Cards sorted first, hands down. Nobody speaks until every table has finished the sort.

blocks.text: Sort the cards, then match them
Six answer lines are on your table.
Sort them into two piles: would gain a mark, and would not.
Then match each losing line to what it is missing. It is the source, the verb or the comparison.
Two lines report well and then add an opinion at the end.
Put those in a third pile and say where the opinion starts.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Checklist face up beside the frame. Marking is done against the list, never against a feeling about the answer.

blocks.text: Marking your own answer
When the writing stops, you become the marker.
A marker does not ask whether the answer is good.
A marker asks whether each line on the checklist can be pointed at.

blocks.caption: The same answer, and only one way of marking it can be checked
blocks.title: Pointing against feeling
blocks.alt: Two boxes compared: a tick placed against a numbered line, and a tick given on a general impression

blocks.text: So every tick carries the line number it was given for.
An untickable line is not a failure. It is the next mark.

items: 1 · tick only what you can point at.
2 · write the line number by each tick.
4 · pick one blank and write the sentence that would fill it.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Pair by table. Two minutes each way, sheets swapped and read in silence.

blocks.text: Check the line numbers
Swap answers and read your partner's ticks.
For each tick, find the line number they wrote.
Go to that line and check it says what the tick claims.
If it does not, ring the tick and hand the sheet back.
You are checking the marking, not the answer.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: Scribe exactly. Do not repair an opinion into a report; mark it untickable and let the pupil change the verb.
stages.data-ta2: A pupil who cannot mark their own answer may read the checklist aloud while an adult places the ticks they name.

blocks.text: Answer, mark it, then name the next mark
Write your answer on your own, using the source sheet and the frame.
Name two sources, and use a reporting verb in each.
Then compare them, and label the point shared or different.
When the time ends, take the checklist and mark your own answer.
Then write the one sentence that would fill your first blank line.

items: Supported · one source reported with the frame, then one tick with its line number.
Standard · two sources reported and compared, then the checklist marked with line numbers.
Stretch · as Standard, and write the sentence that would fill the first blank line.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence
stages.data-ta1: The named adult reads the next-mark sentence back word for word and says which checklist line it would fill.

blocks.text: Read your next-mark line to an adult
Read your next-mark sentence to the adult at your table.
They say which checklist line it would fill.
If it fills none, change the verb before you change the sentence.
Then choose what happens next. Keep it, rewrite the second report, or add a third source.
Write that choice on the sheet with today's date.

sections: The line that would gain the next mark
print.intro: Mark against the checklist, not against how the answer feels. Leave a box blank rather than ticking what you cannot point at.
focusRows: Two sources named, each reported with a reporting verb
One point labelled shared or different
Every tick carrying the line number it was given for
tiers: Report one source using the frame, then place one tick with its line number.
Report and compare two sources, then mark the checklist with line numbers.
As Standard, and write the sentence that would fill the first blank line.
checks: Each report names a source from the approved sheet.
Each report uses a reporting verb, not think, feel or believe.
Every tick carries the line number it was given for.
No sentence states whether the pupil agrees with either source.
